overview: The Kalmar Union linked the crowns of Denmark, Norway and Sweden from 1397, with long interruptions in common rule. Its usual endpoint is Sweden’s separation in 1523, not the atlas’s 1530 boundary. The map also colors all Greenland: that vast shape must not be read as uniform settlement or effective royal control.

periods.title: Margaret’s union
periods.summary: Erik of Pomerania was crowned common king while Margaret retained decisive influence.

periods.title: Strained common monarchy
periods.summary: War and disputes over authority weakened the union’s early arrangement.

periods.title: Repeated separations and reunions
periods.summary: Swedish rulers and councils alternated between cooperation with and resistance to the common crown.

items.text: Margaret built power through Denmark and Norway before Swedish nobles sought her help against King Albert. Her young relative Erik became the shared king in 1397. A ruler could be crowned while someone else still made the most important decisions.

The surviving union letter was written on paper, with corrections and only some expected seals. Historians debate its formal status. It proposed a common ruler and cooperation abroad while each kingdom retained its own laws: joining crowns did not erase legal differences.

Opposition to the union also divided people within Sweden. Powerful families supported different sides, and Engelbrekt’s revolt began in 1434. The story was more complicated than three whole populations always agreeing or disagreeing with one another.

Kalmar had roughly 2,000 inhabitants around 1400, a substantial Swedish town then. Ships carried out iron, butter, cheese and skins and brought back salt, cloth, wine and spices. A harbour connected local kitchens and workshops to distant producers.

The town’s merchants met and celebrated in two houses belonging to the Guild of St Christopher. North of town, a hospice cared for sick and elderly people. Commerce, social gatherings and organized care all occupied identifiable places around the medieval streets.

Kalmar’s church school stood beside St Nicholas’s church. Its schoolmaster in 1430 was Niclis Thoreri, or Nils Thoresson. Boys preparing for trades and commerce learned reading and writing; some future clergy continued to Linköping and even Paris.

Dominican friars helped people draw up purchases and wills as well as preaching. The local hospice charged elderly residents according to their means. These institutions supplied practical services alongside religion: paperwork and care were part of their daily work.

Excavators in Kalmar’s old harbour in the 1930s recovered many medieval gloves and shoes. Oxygen-poor mud protected leather that normally decays. Lost and discarded belongings can reveal everyday clothing more directly than an impressive royal portrait.

In Bergen, Hanseatic merchants traded northern Norwegian stockfish under privileges granted by the crown. Bryggen’s narrow plots joined homes, offices and storage. Its present wooden buildings largely follow rebuilding after 1702, but preserve a layout with medieval roots.

sections.title: A royal pantry and the union’s last years

items.text: King Hans sailed toward a political meeting at Kalmar in 1495, hoping to gain the Swedish crown. His flagship Gribshunden sank off Ronneby. Excavators recovered pepper, cloves, ginger and saffron: the ship carried ingredients suited to an unusually wealthy table.

The wreck’s saffron remained red-orange and released its smell when researchers put it in water. The peppercorns had lost their aroma. Five centuries underwater had treated the contents of this royal spice cupboard very differently.

A wooden barrel on Gribshunden held remains of a sturgeon about two meters long. DNA helped identify the Atlantic species. Researchers connect this prestigious food with the king’s intended display of wealth; it is evidence for an elite voyage, rather than everybody’s dinner.

A preserved copy of Stockholm’s council letter of 28 March 1521 names “Góstaff Ericsson oc hans parti”: “Gustav Eriksson and his party.” The old Swedish spelling belongs to a warning about the rebel later known as Gustav Vasa, not to a modern invented medieval phrase.

Christian II’s coronation celebrations in 1520 were followed by executions of bishops, nobles and townspeople in Stockholm. The violence failed to secure lasting control. Gustav Vasa gathered support and was elected Sweden’s king in 1523, ending the three-crown union.

ending.text: Sweden’s break in 1523 ended the Kalmar Union as a three-kingdom political arrangement. Denmark and Norway remained joined for centuries afterward. Communities, ports, languages and trade continued across the changed political boundaries.
